articles.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
articles.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East By Koh Ewe 
- Published 16 October 2026 
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said. 
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday. 
Beijing has been a long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction". 
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East. 
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran . 
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity. 
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented. 
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe". 
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", he said. 
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East". 
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote. 
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme. 
China itself has been accused of trying to dilute its minority populations by encouraging Han Chinese migration to Tibet, which it annexed in the 1950s, and Xinjiang. Beijing rejects those claims, saying its policies promote economic development and social stability. 
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges. 
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day . More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. 
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. 
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
articles.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea By Koh Ewe   and   Julianna Khan 
- Published 15 October 2026 
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. 
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme. 
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them. 
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty. 
Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties. 
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region. 
The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges". 
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea. 
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC. 
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds. 
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually." 
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why did Xi Jinping visit North Korea? 
But the alliance is not without tension. 
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan. 
China's attitude has shifted more recently. 
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC. 
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war. 
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops. 
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day. 
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties. 
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. 
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. 
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
articles.summary: With the festive season on the horizon, we trace toys from factories in China to US shelves.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US By Sam Fenwick Host – Follow the Money: Business Daily 
- Published 15 October 2026 
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China". 
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external 
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external 
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. 
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes. 
The factory 
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry. 
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting. 
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business. 
- 
Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America 
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed. 
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it." 
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months. 
Image source, Mihox Image caption, 
The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people 
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang. 
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes. 
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it. 
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour. 
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive." 
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises. 
Image source, Mihox Image caption, 
Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price 
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year. 
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so. 
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories. 
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries. 
The ship 
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong. 
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance. 
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September. 
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents. 
The US border 
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). 
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more. 
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents. 
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China. 
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg. 
The US toy company 
Image source, Basic Fun Image caption, 
Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country 
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total. 
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys. 
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says. 
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each. 
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50. 
Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

articles.title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
articles.summary: Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas?
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The recent floods in Nepal have highlighted the need for cross-border co-operation in the Himalayan region By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 15 October 2026 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. 
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. 
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. 
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. 
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. 
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. 
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. 
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? 
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. 
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. 
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. 
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Balendra Shah has urged neighbours India and China to collaborate on climate risks in the Himalayan region 
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development , external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. 
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. 
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. 
And the dangers extend beyond flooding. 
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. 
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. 
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. 
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. 
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. 
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hundreds of people were killed in the deadly flood that tore through the China-Nepal border in August 
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. 
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. 
"What happened after that no one knows," he added. 
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. 
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. 
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. 
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. 
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. 
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. 
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. 
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Experts have raised concerns over climate-related risks as the Himalayan snow cover melts rapidly 
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. 
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. 
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. 
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. 
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. 
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. 
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. 
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

articles.title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
articles.summary: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement By Sharanya Hrishikesh BBC News, Delhi 
- Published 17 October 2026, 01:41 BST 
What is the point of a protest? 
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen? 
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi. 
But that may now be coming to an end. 
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site. 
The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned. 
Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown . 
Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day. 
Delhi Police says , external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford. 
Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed. 
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it 
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand. 
In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions. 
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined. 
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament. 
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament. 
"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper , external . 
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years. 
Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes. 
Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause. 
It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance. 
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra. 
Image source, Courtesy Rachna Dhingra Image caption, 
In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets 
Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme , the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar. 
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says. 
Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise". 
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy. 
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up. 
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests. 
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution. 
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time. 
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying. 
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters. 
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest. 
Those rules have become much stricter , external now. 
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night. 
"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme 
While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture. 
Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance. 
"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says. 
When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said. 
She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar. 
She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law. 
Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi. 
It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site. 
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed". 
As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

articles.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
articles.summary: The US president temporarily ends many restrictions on Moscow recently passed by Congress over "national security" concerns.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters By Max Matza 
- Published 17 October 2026, 03:48 BST Updated 4 hours ago 
Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens. 
The sanctions were passed by the Congress and signed into law the president in September. 
But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions. 
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support. 
Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India. 
It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

- 
Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC 
- Published 23 hours ago 
Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump. 
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment". 
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage", primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations. 
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. 
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. 
A handful of Republicans, too, have come out against the move. 
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Trump ally, called waving sanctions against Russia a mistake, saying on Fox News: "I wish the president hadn't done it." 
He added there were other ways to could address diesel prices and "the current path, unfortunately, just... benefits Putin and that's not a good idea." 
Senator John Cornyn, also of Texas, said on X: "Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next." 
North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", noting the sanctions legislation passed the chamber with bipartisan support and a large majority - only 11 senators voted against it. 
Trump could bring down energy prices "by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin," he said. 
Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said many lawmakers will resist funding the president's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus". 
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort. 
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end". 
He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter." 
Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise? 
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia. 
Negotiators from Ukraine spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week, he also said. 
Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. His Republican party is at risk of losing control of the US Congress, in next month's midterm elections, largely due to voters' sour mood about affordability. 
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. 
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. 
Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military. 
Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries. 
Trump, condemned Ukraine's strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnight 
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. 
Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. 
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning. 
Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues. 
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds. 
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down the network. 
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said. 
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
articles.summary: She and five staff members were found to have used the inedible paint in meals to make them look more appealing.
articles.full_text:
Image caption, 
Kitchen staff was instructed to use inedible paint to enhance the look of meals to attract more students, the court found By Rorey Bosotti 
- Published 17 October 2026, 13:11 BST 
A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food. 
Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media. 
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill. 
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such. 
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported. 
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan. 
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media. 
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff. 
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit. 
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns. 
Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg. 
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization. 
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor. 
China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

articles.title: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
articles.summary: Her public debut as press secretary ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Trump: New White House press secretary should 'reconsider' job By Brandon Drenon Reporting from Washington DC 
- Published 16 October 2026 Updated 17 October 2026 10:14 BST 
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut. 
US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider". 
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters. 
The 42-year-old spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job. 
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter. 
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said. 
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media. 
Hours later, she praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him. 
As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House. 
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X. 
Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president. 
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practise law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam. 
"When I was in China," she replied. 
After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam. 
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials". 
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday. 
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'" 
Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?" 
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning. 
She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one. 
Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?" 
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me." 
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team. 
Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days during Trump's first term. 
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain." 
Prior to her appointment as press secretary, Zacharia was a frequent fixture on right-wing US networks such as Fox and Newsmax. 
She had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and worked as a communications adviser for Trump's social media platform Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn. 
In her early career, Zacharia worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.

articles.title: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
articles.summary: An international rescue operation for the last 30 captive whales in Canada made headlines. Then five of them died.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Toronto Star via Getty Images Image caption, 
Marineland was once an iconic Canadian attraction, known for its Everyone loves Marineland jingle By Max Matza 
- Published 17 October 2026, 02:18 BST 
Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides. 
Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls. 
Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised. 
That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group. 
Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio and even Valencia in Spain. 
Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes. 
Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago and Osorio felt the weight of the moment. 
"This is the last one to happen and it's never going to happen again," he says. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: First beluga whales rescued from closed Marineland park arrive at new homes in the US 
Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin. 
Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has had the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer. 
Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain. 
Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appeared to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago. 
Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease. 
Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died. 
Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. About 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025, according to a tally by the Canadian Press. 
Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes following the death of its longtime owner. 
Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico. 
Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals that includes whales, dolphins and porpoises. 
But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild. 
Image source, Georgia Aquarium Image caption, 
The Georgia aquarium took in two belugas: Balor and Zephyr 
Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands". 
Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales. 
"If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement. 
In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs". 
Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care". 
They said the remaining belugas show positive signs, including eating well. 
World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project. 
As they cannot be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales. 
"I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds. 
The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m). 
But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales. 
One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer. 
"They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state. He adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks. 
"It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild. 
Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity. 
Image source, The Whale Sanctuary Project/ Lori Marino Image caption, 
The Whale Sanctuary Project is constructing a site off the coast of Nova Scotia 
Jason Jones, senior curator of animal wellbeing at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life". 
"Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so." 
Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, seven. They joined the four females already in their care. 
They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says. 
"There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group." 
"They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Former Marineland trainer Phil Demers is an advocate for animal welfare 
Phil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who spoke to the BBC, says the end of Marineland is "bittersweet". 
He's grateful to see the facility shut down and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat. 
He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV. 
"I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says.

articles.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
articles.summary: The Australian government hopes to protect social media users from being served content they don't want to see.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work By Tiffanie Turnbull Sydney 
- Published 16 October 2026 
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder 
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old. 
Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition. 
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day. 
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC. 
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't." 
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words. 
Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBC Image caption, 
Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder 
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week. 
The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow. 
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality. 
Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier. 
But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech. 
The choice 
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral. 
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago. 
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric. 
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order. 
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC. 
"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character." 
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. 
Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC News Image caption, 
Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media 
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man." 
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor. 
Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users. 
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools. 
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture. 
Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction , external ; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health , external , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline . 
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line. 
"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC. 
Image source, Cordelia Hsu/Reuters Image caption, 
Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021 
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change. 
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them. 
Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite. 
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts. 
The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off. 
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said. 
"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them." 
- 
Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears 
- Published 18 August 
- 
Social media is 'deliberately' addictive 
- Published 4 July 2018 
Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Image caption, 
Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill 
The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment". 
Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m). 
"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC. 
The challenges 
There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation. 
In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise . 
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney. 
Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoyment 
Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship. 
But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week. 
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children. 
However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media ban 
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale. 
Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that. 
"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation , external . 
On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return. 
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act. 
Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feeds 
The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app. 
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global. 
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing." 
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them. 
Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment." 
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off. 
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice. 
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good." 
If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line .

Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and scary – Chinese AI
Phillip Inman

In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China 
There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge. 
Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence. 
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by. 
The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries. 
Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level. 
It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again. 
Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square . 
A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule. 
Then came AI and the state discovered complete control. 
Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to. 
Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished. 
For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world. 
Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology. 
Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions. 
Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights. 
Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents. 
There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need. 
Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented . But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option. 
As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation. 
He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.” 
An evaluation report by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship. 
“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says. 
The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities. 
Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assume data inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state . 
The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers. 
Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.
